concepts.title: Bits and Qubits
concepts.simple_explanation: A classical bit is either 0 or 1. A qubit is a two-level quantum system whose state can be a superposition of |0⟩ and |1⟩.
concepts.visual_explanation: Show a classical two-position switch beside a qubit representation; after measurement the qubit produces a classical 0 or 1.
concepts.technical_explanation: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, with |α|² + |β|² = 1. The amplitudes α and β determine measurement probabilities.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is the basic information-representation difference between classical and quantum computing.
concepts.how_it_works: The qubit is manipulated by quantum gates and eventually measured. Measurement produces a classical result.
concepts.common_mistake: Calling a qubit a number between 0 and 1, or saying it literally stores two classical values.
concepts.connection: Builds directly on Topic 1.1's introduction to qubits and measurement.
concepts.try_it: Prepare |0⟩, apply H, and measure repeatedly.
concepts.key_takeaway: A qubit has a quantum state described by amplitudes; measurement gives a classical 0 or 1.

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.simple_explanation: Superposition means a quantum state can be a linear combination of basis states.
concepts.visual_explanation: Display |0⟩ and |1⟩ as basis states and a vector/state that has components along both.
concepts.example: Starting from |0⟩, applying H produces equal amplitudes for |0⟩ and |1⟩, giving 50% probability for each on measurement.
concepts.why_it_matters: Superposition is one of the resources quantum algorithms manipulate, but it is not by itself a useful brute-force readout of all answers.
concepts.how_it_works: A quantum gate changes amplitudes coherently; later gates and measurement determine how those amplitudes interfere and what can be observed.
concepts.common_mistake: Saying a qubit simply stores both 0 and 1 as two readable classical values.
concepts.try_it: Apply H to |0⟩, then measure 20 times.
concepts.key_takeaway: Superposition is a quantum state description, not two ordinary bits stored in one place.

concepts.title: Measurement
concepts.simple_explanation: Measuring a single qubit returns a classical 0 or 1.
concepts.visual_explanation: Use probability bars for P(0) and P(1), then show one sampled outcome per shot.
concepts.technical_explanation: For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, P(0)=|α|² and P(1)=|β|². Measurement changes the state to the observed basis state in the ideal projective-measurement picture.
concepts.example: For α=√3/2 and β=1/2, repeated shots approach 75% 0 and 25% 1.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why quantum computation cannot simply expose every amplitude as readable classical data.
concepts.how_it_works: Each shot produces one classical outcome; repeating the experiment estimates the underlying distribution.
concepts.common_mistake: Thinking one measurement returns the full statevector.
concepts.connection: Links superposition to observable probabilities and to the 2^n state-space discussion.
concepts.try_it: Run 1, 10, 100, and 1000 shots for H|0⟩ and compare the histogram.
concepts.key_takeaway: Quantum states can contain many amplitudes, but measurement gives a classical outcome.

concepts.title: Logic Gates vs Quantum Gates
concepts.simple_explanation: Classical logic gates such as AND, OR, and NOT process classical bits. Quantum gates such as X, H, Z, and CNOT transform quantum states.
concepts.visual_explanation: Compare a classical AND truth table with a reversible quantum gate such as H.
concepts.technical_explanation: Ideal quantum gates are unitary transformations satisfying U†U=I, so they are reversible. H·H=I.
concepts.example: X flips |0⟩ to |1⟩ and |1⟩ to |0⟩. H creates equal superposition from |0⟩.
concepts.why_it_matters: It explains why quantum circuits are built differently from ordinary Boolean logic circuits.
concepts.how_it_works: A quantum gate acts linearly on amplitudes and preserves normalization.
concepts.common_mistake: Assuming every quantum gate creates superposition.
concepts.connection: Connects gates to interference and circuit evolution.
concepts.try_it: Compare X|0⟩, H|0⟩, and Z|0⟩ in the simulator.
concepts.key_takeaway: Quantum gates are reversible/unitary state transformations; they are not just quantum versions of AND/OR.

concepts.title: Interference
concepts.simple_explanation: Quantum amplitudes can reinforce or cancel one another. This is interference.
concepts.visual_explanation: Contrast a classical random 50/50 bit with H→H on |0⟩, where the final probability becomes 100% for 0.
concepts.technical_explanation: H|0⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and applying H again gives |0⟩. The relative signs/phases of amplitudes allow constructive and destructive interference.
concepts.example: H followed by H returns |0⟩, whereas a classical random bit that is independently sampled does not become deterministic merely because you 'flip' it twice.
concepts.why_it_matters: Interference is central to how quantum algorithms amplify useful outcomes and suppress others.
concepts.how_it_works: Later gates combine amplitude contributions; signs and phases determine whether they add or cancel.
concepts.common_mistake: Treating a quantum superposition as just a classical random coin.
concepts.connection: Connects superposition to algorithmic advantage and measurement.
concepts.try_it: Run H-H, H-Z-H, and H-X-H on |0⟩.
concepts.key_takeaway: Superposition supplies amplitudes; interference controls how those amplitudes combine.

concepts.title: Multiple Qubits and Exponential State Space
concepts.simple_explanation: An n-qubit state is described by 2^n complex amplitudes.
concepts.visual_explanation: Show a counter or growth chart: 1 qubit→2 amplitudes, 2→4, 3→8, 10→1024, 50→2^50.
concepts.technical_explanation: |Ψ⟩=Σ_x c_x|x⟩ over 2^n computational-basis states, with Σ|c_x|²=1.
concepts.example: 50 qubits require 2^50 = 1,125,899,906,842,624 amplitudes. At 16 bytes per complex amplitude, the simple dense-state estimate is 16 PiB.
concepts.why_it_matters: This explains why general-purpose classical statevector simulation becomes difficult as qubit count grows.
concepts.how_it_works: Each added qubit doubles the dimension of the statevector.
concepts.common_mistake: Saying 50 qubits let you read 2^50 classical numbers from one measurement.
concepts.connection: Connects measurement limits to classical simulation cost.
concepts.try_it: Predict the amplitude count for 30 qubits, then estimate memory at 16 bytes per amplitude.
concepts.key_takeaway: The quantum state dimension grows exponentially, while measurement still returns only a classical outcome string.

concepts.title: Entanglement
concepts.simple_explanation: Entanglement is a joint quantum state that cannot be written as independent states of the individual qubits.
concepts.visual_explanation: Show H on q0 followed by CNOT(q0,q1), then a probability table with 00 and 11 at 50% each.
concepts.technical_explanation: The Bell state |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 is entangled. Measuring one qubit gives correlated results with the other, but this does not enable faster-than-light communication.
concepts.example: Starting from |00⟩, H(q0) then CNOT(q0,q1) produces the Bell state; ideal outcomes are 00 and 11 only.
concepts.why_it_matters: Entanglement is a distinct quantum resource used by many quantum algorithms and protocols.
concepts.how_it_works: A multi-qubit state develops correlations that cannot be represented as a product of separate single-qubit states.
concepts.common_mistake: Thinking entanglement is a communication channel that sends usable information faster than light.
concepts.connection: Uses superposition, CNOT, and measurement together.
concepts.try_it: Run the Bell circuit for 1000 shots and inspect the outcome histogram.
concepts.key_takeaway: Entanglement creates non-classical correlations, not faster-than-light messaging.

concepts.title: What Quantum Computers Are and Aren't Good At
concepts.simple_explanation: Quantum computers are expected to help on particular problem classes; they are not universally faster than classical computers.
concepts.visual_explanation: Use a problem-type table: factoring, unstructured search, quantum simulation, NP-complete problems, everyday tasks.
concepts.technical_explanation: Shor's algorithm gives a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for integer factoring on an ideal fault-tolerant quantum computer; Grover gives roughly √N query scaling for unstructured search. No efficient quantum algorithm for NP-complete problems is known.
concepts.example: Grover changes unstructured search from roughly N queries classically to roughly √N quantum queries in the query model.
concepts.why_it_matters: It prevents the central misconception that quantum computing is simply a faster replacement for classical computing.
concepts.how_it_works: Speedups arise from specific algorithms that exploit quantum structure such as interference and entanglement.
concepts.common_mistake: Assuming any workload gets a quantum speedup.
concepts.connection: Builds on all preceding concepts and leads into Topic 1.3 applications.
concepts.try_it: Classify web browsing, database lookup, factoring, unstructured search, and quantum simulation by whether a quantum advantage is established/expected by the source.
concepts.key_takeaway: Quantum advantage is problem- and algorithm-specific.
